content: Integrated testing for other diseases, such as sexually transmitted infections (STIs) and viral hepatitis, can be combined with HIV testing services. It is essential to ensure that staff involved in these testing services possess the necessary skills and proficiency to perform the tests accurately. Diagnostic assays that lack good thermostability, unlike rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs) which can be stored between 4°C and 40°C, and those requiring more invasive specimen collection methods (e.g., venepuncture instead of capillary or fingerstick whole blood) are not suitable for use in lower-tier healthcare settings (levels 1 and 0). For further details on assay formats for HIV diagnosis, refer to the 2019 WHO Consolidated Guidelines on HIV Testing Services, Web Annex I. The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends a three-test strategy for HIV diagnosis. Without this approach, programs cannot ensure a positive predictive value (PPV) of at least 99%, which is critical to minimizing HIV misdiagnoses to fewer than 1 in 100 individuals. This strategy aligns with the WHO Essential In Vitro Diagnostics List (EDL), which outlines assays for common diseases and infections in both community settings without clinical laboratories and health facilities with laboratory capabilities. The performance of diagnostic assays is measured by sensitivity and specificity. However, these metrics alone do not provide sufficient information about the clinical value of test results. Additional data is required to determine the predictive value of assays used within a testing algorithm. PPV refers to the proportion of individuals with positive test results who are correctly diagnosed with HIV, while negative predictive value (NPV) refers to the proportion of individuals with negative results who are correctly identified as HIV-negative. Unlike sensitivity and specificity, PPV and NPV are influenced by the prevalence of the disease in the population being tested. To achieve a PPV of at least 99%, WHO recommends selecting tests with a minimum sensitivity of 99% and specificity of 98%. In a three-test strategy, at least three consecutive reactive HIV tests are required to confirm an HIV-positive diagnosis. This strategy applies to individuals aged 18 months and older and can utilize various serology assay formats, such as RDTs or immunoassays (IAs), but excludes Western blot and line immunoassays, which WHO advises against using. The three-test strategy involves the following steps: 1. All individuals are tested using Assay 1 (A1). Non-reactive results (A1−) are reported as HIV-negative. 2. Reactive results on A1 (A1+) are followed by testing with a separate and distinct Assay 2 (A2). 3. Individuals reactive on both A1 and A2 (A1+; A2+) are tested with a separate and distinct Assay 3 (A3). If A3 is reactive (A1+; A2+; A3+), the individual is reported as HIV-positive. If A3 is non-reactive (A1+; A2+; A3−), the result is reported as HIV-inconclusive, and the individual is asked to return in 14 days for additional testing. If an individual is reactive on A1 but non-reactive on A2 (A1+; A2−), A1 should be repeated: If the repeat A1 is non-reactive (A1+; A2−; repeat A1−), the result is reported as HIV-negative. If the repeat A1 is reactive (A1+; A2−; repeat A1+), the result is reported as HIV-inconclusive, and the individual is asked to return in 14 days for further testing. After an HIV-positive diagnosis, WHO advises retesting to verify the diagnosis before initiating antiretroviral therapy (ART). This retesting serves as a quality assurance measure to prevent unnecessary lifelong treatment. In Malawi, transitioning to a three-test strategy has been instrumental in maintaining a PPV of at least 99%. This approach has prevented numerous misdiagnoses and unnecessary treatment, resulting in significant cost savings for the healthcare system and reducing the social and individual burden of misdiagnosis. For example, in 2023, at least 371 individuals in select facilities would have been misdiagnosed and incorrectly started on lifelong treatment without the three-test strategy. For children aged 18 months or younger, serology assays alone, such as HIV RDTs, are insufficient for diagnosis due to the potential detection of maternal antibodies transferred during pregnancy. Virological testing, typically using nucleic acid testing (NAT), is recommended for diagnosing HIV in this age group. NAT should be offered at birth, 4–6 weeks, 9 months, and 18 months or 3 months after breastfeeding cessation. Retesting after a positive NAT result is crucial to avoid unnecessary treatment, particularly in settings with low transmission rates.
